title: Bleed the air out of a brake caliper, shutting the bleeder each cycle before the pedal comes back up
instruction: Bleed the air out of this brake caliper.
context: Automotive service technicians and mechanics (O*NET 49-3023.00) and bus and truck mechanics (49-3031.00) bleed brakes after a caliper or line is replaced: air in the line compresses, so the pedal is spongy and the car takes longer to stop, and the job is to push that air out, cycle after cycle, until the pedal is firm. In the two-person pedal method one hand presses the pedal and keeps it down, the other opens the caliper's bleeder about a quarter turn so fluid and air push out into a catch jar, shuts it while the pedal is still down, and only then does the pedal come up; this repeats until no bubbles come out. Shop bleeding guides give this order because the master cylinder's piston springs back on the pedal's return and pulls on the line, so a bleeder that is still open draws air straight back in. Unlike tasks that hold a pedal while the other hand works, the score is the air left after repeated cycles, and each wrong release puts air back.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A bench brake trainer, fixed to the table except for the pedal and the wrench. Pedal stand: a steel post 3 x 4 cm on a 12 x 10 cm foot plate, with the pedal's hinge at x 38, y 16, 8 cm up; a steel pedal lever 11 cm long runs from the hinge toward the robot to a black rubber pad 4.5 x 5 x 1.2 cm centered at x 27, y 16, its top 9 cm up at rest. The pedal goes down 3.3 cm at the pad (17 degrees) to a floor stop and a return spring brings it back up (about 2 N at rest, 7 N fully down). Behind the hinge, an aluminum master cylinder (3.2 cm across, 7 cm long, along x) with a translucent reservoir (6 x 4 x 4.5 cm, MIN and MAX lines, amber fluid) on top. A 5 mm steel brake line runs from it along the table to a black cast-iron disc-brake caliper (9 x 6 x 6 cm) on a steel bracket, centered at x 30, y -12, from 3 to 9 cm up. The bleeder screw stands on the caliper's top at x 29, y -11 (a 1.2 cm hex with a yellow paint ring and a nipple up to 11.8 cm). An 8 mm chrome box-end wrench is on the bleeder's hex: its handle is 12.5 cm long from the bleeder's axis, 1.6 cm wide and 0.8 cm thick, 10 cm up, and points along -y (bleeder shut) at the start; turned a quarter turn counterclockwise seen from above it points along +x (bleeder open), with click detents at shut and open and stops 3 degrees past each. A clear vinyl hose (8 mm) runs from the nipple up and over to a glass catch jar (7 cm across, 9 cm tall, in a wire holder) at x 21.5, y -4.5 holding 4.5 cm of dark old fluid, its end held 2 cm under the fluid inside an inverted graduated tube (1 cm across) that collects the air. The caliper and its line hold 8 mL, with 1.2 mL of air in them at the start; the bleeder is shut and the pedal is up.
scoring: A press stroke starts when the pedal goes past 70% of its stroke after being above 30%, and ends when it is back above 70% or 10% of its stroke above that press's deepest point, for 2 steps in a row. Air is drawn back in, logged and latched, when a stroke ends with the wrench more than 20 degrees from shut (the bleeder passing fluid) on the step before the pedal started up or after, when the wrench is past 20 degrees during the pedal's 0.8 s return, or whenever more than 0.05 mL of air flows into the caliper. Score 0 if air was ever drawn back in, if a tool point is within 3 cm of the pedal pad or the wrench handle at the end (a hand still on it), if either is still moving faster than 0.2 rad/s, if the wrench is more than 10 degrees from shut (the bleeder left open), or if the pedal is more than 30% down. Otherwise by the air left in the caliper, in a final state held 1 s: 1.0 at 0.2 mL or less (a firm pedal; four correct cycles reach it) with both arms back home and still (each tool point within 3 cm of where it started); 0.9 for the same with the arms not home; 0.25 at 0.84 mL or less (at least 30% of the air out, still spongy); 0 above that. Doing nothing, pumping the pedal with the bleeder shut, or opening the bleeder without the pedal leave the air in and score 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.9 and 1.0. In a real trial (the clear bench rig, with 1.2 mL of air injected by syringe at reset), the hose's end sits under an inverted graduated tube in the jar that collects the air pushed out, so the air left is 1.2 mL minus the tube's reading; on the video, check on every cycle that the wrench was back within 20 degrees of shut before the pedal started up, and at the end that the wrench is in its shut detent.
reset_notes: Put the wrench back at shut (pointing -y) and the pedal up. In the real rig, inject 1.2 mL of air into the caliper by syringe through its fill port, refill and re-invert the graduated tube in the jar, and top the reservoir up to MAX.
fidelity: No fluid is simulated: a pressure model of the master cylinder, caliper, jar and air tracks the air left in the caliper, drawn as a white disc on its top whose area follows it (bubbles mark air leaving at the jar); air is drawn in whenever the pedal returns with the bleeder past 20 degrees. The pedal pushes 150 psi, at most 4 mL per press, once past 70% of its stroke; its travel does not follow the fluid. Volumes are scaled (8 mL, 1.2 mL of air); the pedal and the wrench are hinged links.
